body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Night-shift nurse staffing and hospital-acquired pressure injuries: an observational study across 24 medical wards","authors":"Achterberg-Kimani L, Solberg-Nwosu P, Fairley-Ortega D","year":2020,"venue":"Skerrow Journal of Nursing Workforce","doi":"10.5555/sjnw.2020.0419","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked shift-level staffing records to hospital-acquired pressure injuries on 24 medical wards over two years. Each additional patient per registered nurse on night shifts was associated with an 11 percent higher incidence of category 2 or worse pressure injuries after adjustment for patient acuity and ward. Day-shift staffing showed a weaker association. The association was strongest on wards where most patients were at high risk. Because staffing and acuity move together, residual confounding is likely, and the study cannot show that a fixed ratio would prevent injuries. Wards with a float nurse available at night had fewer missed repositioning episodes recorded in care plans."},{"title":"Protected night repositioning rounds on two medical wards: a before-after improvement report","authors":"Mwale-Lindgren C, Oyelaran-Pike T","year":2022,"venue":"Greyhaven Improvement Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two medical wards introduced protected night repositioning rounds at fixed times, led by a named nurse, with a float nurse joining when staffing fell below a set level. We compared pressure injuries in the nine months before and the nine months after the change. Category 2 or worse injuries fell from 3.1 to 1.9 per 1,000 patient-days. Completion of the night rounds was recorded on 84 percent of nights. Nurses reported that fixed times made repositioning harder to postpone. The comparison is uncontrolled, a new mattress contract started during the second period, and injuries were counted from incident reports."},{"title":"Pressure injury prevention bundles in acute hospital care: a systematic review","authors":"Kaur-Brennan S, Delacroix-Ansah M, Petrov-Holt J, Nakashima-Obi F","year":2019,"venue":"Lowbridge Acute Care Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/lacq.2019.0288","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases for controlled and uncontrolled studies of prevention bundles in adult acute care. Thirty-one studies met the criteria; 26 reported fewer pressure injuries after a bundle was introduced, but only five had a concurrent control. Repositioning schedules, risk reassessment and skin inspection were the most common components. Effects were larger in studies that measured injuries by incident reports than in studies that used direct skin inspection. Most studies were at high risk of bias, and none separated the effect of staffing from the effect of the bundle. The review supports bundles as change ideas rather than as proven interventions."},{"title":"Weekly skin inspection compared with incident reporting for measuring pressure injury incidence","authors":"Varga-Adebayo H, Lindqvist-Sato R","year":2017,"venue":"Skerrow Journal of Nursing Workforce","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On six wards we compared pressure injuries found at weekly skin inspection by a tissue viability nurse with injuries recorded in the incident reporting system. Incident reports captured 64 percent of the category 2 or worse injuries found at inspection. Capture was lower for injuries on the heels and for patients discharged within a week. Reporting rose during periods of improvement activity, which would make an improvement project look worse at first when measured by incident reports. The authors recommend weekly inspection as the outcome measure for improvement work and incident reports as a secondary source."},{"title":"Float nurse deployment when night ratios exceed a threshold: effects on missed care in medical wards","authors":"Ferreira-Mbeki A, Holm-Quartey S","year":2024,"venue":"Greyhaven Improvement Letters","doi":"10.5555/gil.2024.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Four medical wards deployed a float nurse on nights when the ratio exceeded one nurse to seven patients. Using care-plan records, we compared missed care on nights with and without a float nurse over one year. Missed repositioning was recorded on 18 percent of high-risk patient-nights without a float nurse and 9 percent with one. Missed medication doses showed a similar but smaller difference. Float nurses were available on 61 percent of the nights that met the threshold. Nights were not allocated at random, and ward managers requested float nurses more often for the busiest nights."},{"title":"Skin tone and the detection of early pressure injury: an observational study of nurse assessment","authors":"Okonkwo-Reyes B, Tanaka-Whitfield G","year":2021,"venue":"Lowbridge Acute Care Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/lacq.2021.0045","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared ward nurses' skin assessments with assessments by tissue viability specialists in 540 adult inpatients. Category 1 pressure injuries were missed by ward nurses in 38 percent of patients with darker skin tones and 14 percent of patients with lighter skin tones. Missed early injuries more often progressed to category 2 or worse within a week. Assessment that included touch for warmth and firmness, not only colour, reduced the difference. The study used a small number of specialist assessors in one hospital, and skin tone was recorded by the assessors."},{"title":"Run chart rules for rare adverse events in ward improvement projects","authors":"Brandt-Osei K, Marsh-Nakamura E","year":2015,"venue":"Greyhaven Improvement Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Improvement teams often plot rare adverse events such as pressure injuries or falls with injury as weekly counts, which produces charts dominated by zeros. We simulated ward-level data and compared run charts of weekly rates with charts of the number of patient-days between events. With fewer than two events per ward per week, charts of patient-days between events detected a halving of the event rate about six weeks earlier than weekly run charts and gave fewer false signals. We recommend charts of time or patient-days between events for rare events, with the counting rule fixed before baseline."}]}
